title: Research
text: I have two broad research interests related to the linguistic sub-fields of speech perception and computational linguistics.

title: Research
text:
Vowel Perception
My dissertation research focuses on investigating how modulation in fundamental frequency (F0) and higher formants (F3-F5) affects the perception of vowel quality in English by examining listeners’ perceptual behavior. Some questions that I hope to answer through this work include how F0 and the higher formants affect the perceptual dimensions of F1 (vowel height) and F2 (vowel frontness) and how listeners’ perceptual categorization boundaries shift according to these manipulations. Through my work I hope to better understand the nature and magnitude of F0- and the higher formant-induced perceptual shifts in reference to the uniform scaling hypothesis and the Probabilistic Sliding Template Model of Vowel Perception (PSTM).
My other work in speech perception has focused on how socio-indexical information affects perceptual decisions in L1 and L2 contexts. My qualifying paper for my Ph.D. in Linguistics investigated how listeners use the socio-indexical information of apparent gender to inform the perceptual weighting of vowel duration and its effect on the perception of voicing for coda stops in English. In addition, I have conducted experimental research that investigates the perception of contrastive vowel quantity for L2 Japanese speakers.

title: Research
section: Applications of Large Language Models to Language Learning and Assessment
text:
Applications of Large Language Models to Language Learning and Assessment
Given my background in teaching English both as a foreign and second language, I am interested in applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to issues related to second language teaching.
Currently, I am interested in leveraging CEFR descriptors and writing rubrics to train models that can reliably perform level placement.
I have also completed and published research that focused on leveraging LLMs for the purpose of detecting and improving coherence in the writing of English language learners, and co-authored a paper for the 2024 EMNLP.

title: About
text:
I am an Associate Professor in the English Program for Global Mobility at the University of Nagano and a Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Linguistics at UC Davis working with Dr. Santiago Barreda.

I hold a Master of Arts in Linguistics from UC Davis, a Bachelor of Arts in Japanese, and a Master of Science in Education (TESOL) both from California State University, Fullerton. In addition to these academic degrees, I have over 12 years of language teaching experience both in the U.S. and abroad in Japan.
